newsitem.title: HONG KONG: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Philippines fazed by market.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Philippines fazed by market.

text.p: The Central Bank of the Philippines surprised Asian debt markets on Wednesday by postponing its long-awaited Yankee bond.

As recently as yesterday, the central bank said it would launch up to US $1.0 billion of bonds in tranches of 30 to 100 years on April 15, despite criticism in congress that the issue would result in an increase in the country's foreign debt and interest payments.
But the issue failed to materialize and the issuer blamed the no-show on poor market conditions.

"Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas led by Governor Gabriel C. Singson has decided to reset the timing of the launch of its Yankee bond offering due to the highly unfavorable bond market conditions in the last few days," the central bank said in a statement.

U.S. stocks and bonds have sold off recently as strong U.S. economic data -- notably the March producer price index revealed last Friday -- have heightened fears that the Federal Reserve would raise interest rates again to ward off inflation.
Price talk on the Philippines' 30-year tranche had widened to 212-225 basis points over Treasuries from 200 basis points a few weeks ago, traders in Hong Kong noted.
Analysts in the Philippines said the BSP was probably wise to postpone the issue, given the state of the U.S. market and a less voracious appetite recently for Philippine paper.
"I think it is a wise decision on the governor's part," said Andrew Alcid, head of capital markets at Citibank in Manila.
"If all they wanted to do was to raise money they probably could have shortened the tenor and got a deal done but that's not what they really wanted to do," said Alcid.

The Kingdom of Thailand scrapped plans to launch at 30-year bond and stuck with a 10-year tenor when it sold its Yankee issue last week. The move was at least partially because of the poor market for longer-dated issues.

(Thailand's bond has since tightened in the secondary market. But traders pointed out that because the sovereign deal priced wide, spreads on other Thai bonds have adjusted to the new sovereign benchmark by widening.)
The Philippines already has 20-year paper in the market and was seen as keen on extending its benchmark yield curve.
But some traders in Hong Kong said they were perplexed by the central bank's action, noting that the U.S. Treasury market rallied Tuesday following benign retail price data.
The U.S. Treasury's benchmark 30-year bond rose 30/32 to 94-8/32 to yield 7.09 percent versus 7.17 percent on Monday.
"I don't know why the Philippines postponed it. Yesterday, the market was up and they missed an opportunity," said one Hong Kong trader.
In other news, Union Bank of Hong Kong has launched a HK$500 million floating rate certificate of deposit issue. Schroders Asia and Jardine Fleming are lead managers.

Bankers said the pricing was reasonable and the deal was attractive for relationship purposes. The borrower is majority owned by China Merchants Holdings and the issue includes an ownership maintenance covenant.
Bank Rakyat Indonesia launched a US$70 million FRCD due March 2002 that is fungible with a previous issue.

Traders said news that Standard and Poor's Corp had affirmed the long-term counterparty ratings of Bank of Ayudhya but had cut its short-term counterpary ratings had no affect on the bank's issues traded in the secondary market.
